design_concepts.name: Export Iteration for ER Evaluation
design_concepts.description: Methodology for computing entity resolution statistics by iterating the SDK export stream. Use export_json_entity_report with SZ_EXPORT_DEFAULT_FLAGS to get all resolved entities. Each exported row is a JSON object containing RESOLVED_ENTITY (with ENTITY_ID, RECORDS[], ENTITY_NAME) and RELATED_ENTITIES[] (with ENTITY_ID, MATCH_LEVEL_CODE, MATCH_KEY, ERRULE_CODE, RECORD_SUMMARY[]). MATCH_LEVEL_CODE values in RELATED_ENTITIES: POSSIBLY_SAME (strong but inconclusive match), POSSIBLY_RELATED (weaker association), DISCLOSED_RELATION (explicitly declared relationship). IMPORTANT: Each relationship appears in BOTH entities' RELATED_ENTITIES — deduplicate by sorting (min_id, max_id) pairs and using a set. Compute all statistics in a single pass over the export stream and output as JSON for downstream evaluation. SCALING NOTE: Export iteration is O(all entities) — fine for thousands of entities, slow for millions, and impractical for billions. This approach is suitable for POC evaluation and small datasets. For production scale, the scalable alternative is to use INFO messages from add_record, which provide real-time affected entity IDs. Feed these into an incremental data mart that updates only changed entities. See the data_mart topic for the production pattern using SZ_WITH_INFO and AFFECTED_ENTITIES.
computes: Per data source: record count, entity count, compression rate (1 - entities/records)
Cross-source overlap: entities spanning multiple sources, count per source pair
Entity size distribution: 1, 2, 3-5, 6-10, 11-50, 51+ record buckets with entity counts
Match principle frequency: ERRULE_CODE + MATCH_KEY combinations with counts
Relationship categories: POSSIBLY_SAME, POSSIBLY_RELATED, DISCLOSED_RELATION counts (deduplicated)
Top match principles per source pair for cross-source entities
Sample entity IDs for each size bucket (up to 5 per bucket)
Output as JSON with all metrics for programmatic evaluation

design_concepts.name: 4-Point ER Evaluation Framework
design_concepts.description: A structured methodology for evaluating entity resolution quality that requires concrete evidence at every step. The framework prevents hallucinated assessments by demanding that the evaluator show specific records and entities to support each finding. Apply after loading test data and collecting statistics.
steps:
SANITY CHECK: Compare compression rates against source profiler uniqueness stats from the data profiling step. If the profiler showed 95% unique names but compression is 50%, that is suspicious over-matching. If profiler showed 30% duplicate names but compression is only 2%, likely under-matching. Zero relationships in a multi-source load is a red flag — features may not be mapping correctly.
OVER-MATCHING: Review entity size distribution. Examine sample multi-record entities from the 3+, 10+, and 50+ buckets. For each sampled entity, SHOW THE RECORDS to the user — display the actual data from each record in the entity. Are the merged records the same real-world person/org, or are different people forced together by generic features (common name + common city)? Evidence: entity ID, record count, records with source data.
UNDER-MATCHING: Check the possible match (POSSIBLY_SAME) queue. Review sample pairs from the queue. For each pair, SHOW THE EVIDENCE — what features matched and what was missing that prevented full resolution. If many near-misses are concentrated on one match key pattern, this likely indicates a mapping issue (e.g., phone numbers not mapped). Evidence: entity pair IDs, match keys, sample records from both entities.
MATCH PRINCIPLES: Do the top match keys (ERRULE_CODE + MATCH_KEY) align with the features that were mapped? Cross-reference with the analyzer report from the generate step. If NAME+DOB is the top match key but ADDRESS was also mapped, check whether ADDRESS appears in any match keys — if not, there may be data quality issues with the address data. Evidence: match key frequency table, mapped features list.

design_concepts.name: Evidence Requirement for ER Evaluation
design_concepts.description: CRITICAL: Every evaluation finding MUST be supported by specific evidence — actual records, entity IDs, and data values. This is the hallucination-prevention mechanism. An LLM can easily generate plausible-sounding evaluation narratives without actually examining the data. By requiring that every claim references specific entity IDs and shows the actual record data, we force the evaluation to be grounded in reality. Bad: "The resolution quality looks good with reasonable compression rates." Good: "Entity 1042 contains 3 records from CUSTOMERS and 1 from VENDORS. Records CUST-001 (John Smith, 1985-03-15, 555-1234) and CUST-047 (J. Smith, 1985-03-15, 555-1234) correctly resolved via +NAME+DOB+PHONE. Record VEND-203 (Smith Consulting, 555-1234) merged via +PHONE only — this is suspicious and may be over-matching."
steps: Every claim about over-matching must reference specific entity IDs and show record data
Every claim about under-matching must reference specific entity pair IDs and match evidence
Every claim about match quality must reference the actual match key frequency data
Never make qualitative statements without citing specific numbers from the stats

sdk_patterns_notes: Single-pass over the export stream — memory-efficient for large datasets.
Relationships are deduplicated using (min_id, max_id) pairs since each relationship appears in both entities.
Output is JSON for programmatic consumption by the evaluation framework.
compression_rate = 1 - (entities/records): 0 means no dedup, 0.5 means 50% compression.

anti_patterns.pattern: Evaluating ER quality without reviewing sample entities
anti_patterns.correct: Never assess ER quality from aggregate statistics alone. Always retrieve and show specific records from multi-record entities, possible match pairs, and large entities. The evidence requirement prevents hallucinated evaluations.

anti_patterns.pattern: Comparing compression rates without baseline from profiler
anti_patterns.correct: Compression rates are meaningless without context. Compare against the source data profiler results from step 1 — if the profiler showed 95% unique names, 50% compression is suspicious. If it showed 30% duplicate names, 50% compression may be expected.

anti_patterns.pattern: Ignoring the possible match queue during evaluation
anti_patterns.correct: Under-matching is as important as over-matching. Always check the POSSIBLY_SAME queue — if many near-misses share the same match key pattern, a feature is likely unmapped or has data quality issues. Possible matches are the primary signal for under-matching.
